Unit I · Introduction to AI Tools

+

AI means Artificial Intelligence. Artificial means made by humans. Intelligence means the ability to learn, understand and solve problems.

+

So AI is a computer program that can do things which normally need human intelligence. For example:

+
  • Understanding your voice when you say "Ok Google".
  • Finding your friend's face in a photo.
  • Suggesting the next video on YouTube.
  • Finding the fastest route from Gajuwaka to RK Beach on Google Maps.
  • Writing an email when you give it a few words.

+

A normal program follows fixed rules written by a programmer. An AI program learns from examples. This is the big difference.

+

AI is not new. Here is a very short history.

+
  • 1950: Alan Turing asked, "Can machines think?" He suggested a test. If a machine can chat like a human, we can call it intelligent.
  • 1956: The name "Artificial Intelligence" was used for the first time at a meeting in Dartmouth, USA.
  • 1960s to 1980s: Early AI used rules written by experts. It worked for small problems. It failed for big ones. People lost interest. This time is called the "AI winter".
  • 1997: IBM's Deep Blue computer beat the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov.
  • 2012: A new method called deep learning became very good at seeing images. AI started to grow fast.
  • 2017: Google researchers made the Transformer. This is the design used by ChatGPT and Gemini today.
  • 2022: ChatGPT was released. In two months, 100 million people used it. This started the Generative AI wave.
  • Today: AI can write, draw, talk, code and even make videos.
+Narrow AIDoes one job wellGoogle Maps, spam filter, face unlock
+Generative AICreates new text, images, audio or codeChatGPT, Gemini
+General AI (AGI)Can do any task a human can doDoes not exist yet

+

All the AI we use today is narrow AI or generative AI. AGI is still a dream.

+

Why should an engineer learn AI tools?

+

You will use AI tools in every branch. A civil engineer can ask AI to check a report. A mechanical engineer can ask AI to write a Python script to read sensor data. A chemical engineer can ask AI to explain a reaction. AI tools are like a calculator. They do not replace you. They make you faster.

+
Think of AI as a smart helper. It is fast and knows many things. But it can make mistakes. You are the engineer. You must check its work.

+
  • Open chatgpt.com or gemini.google.com. Type: "Explain AI to a first year engineering student in Visakhapatnam in 5 simple sentences."
  • Ask the same tool: "Give 5 examples of AI that I use every day on my phone."
  • Watch this short video: What is AI? – CrashCourse.

+
  • Artificial — made by humans, not natural.
  • Intelligence — the ability to learn, understand and solve problems.
  • Program — a set of instructions that a computer follows.
  • Rule — a fixed instruction like "if X then do Y".
  • Deep learning — a way for computers to learn from a lot of examples, using many layers of maths.
  • Transformer — the design (architecture) used inside ChatGPT and Gemini.
  • Narrow AI — AI that does only one kind of job.
  • AGI — Artificial General Intelligence; an AI that can do anything a human can. Not real yet.

+

Unit I · Introduction to AI Tools

+

Most AI today works in three steps.

+
  1. Data. We collect many examples. For example, 10,000 photos of cats and 10,000 photos of dogs.
  2. Training. The computer looks at the examples again and again. It slowly adjusts numbers inside itself until it gets most answers right. The result is called a model.
  3. Prediction. We give the model a new photo. It says "cat" or "dog". This is called a prediction, or an output.

+

The whole method is called Machine Learning (ML). The machine learns from data. Nobody writes the rules by hand.

+

Suppose you want to predict the price of a flat in Madhurawada. You collect data: size of the flat, floor, distance from the beach and the price. You give this data to an ML model. It learns the pattern. Then you give it a new flat. It predicts the price.

+

The model is not magic. It only finds patterns in the data you gave it. If your data is bad, the model is bad. There is a saying: garbage in, garbage out.
+Supervised learningData has the correct answers (labels)Photos labelled "cat" or "dog"
+Unsupervised learningData has no labels; the model finds groupsGrouping customers by what they buy
+Reinforcement learningThe model gets a reward when it does wellA game-playing AI, a robot learning to walk

+

A neural network is a type of model. It is loosely inspired by the brain. It has many small units called neurons, arranged in layers. Each neuron does a small calculation. Together, millions of them can learn very complex patterns.

+

When a network has many layers, we call it deep learning. Deep learning is behind almost all modern AI: voice assistants, face unlock, self-driving cars and ChatGPT.

+
  • A lot of data (the whole internet, in some cases).
  • A lot of computers with special chips called GPUs.
  • A lot of electricity and money.

+

This is why only big companies like Google, OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic train the largest models. But anyone can use them. That is what this course is about.

+
  • Play Quick, Draw! by Google. You draw. The AI guesses. Every drawing becomes training data.
  • Try Teachable Machine. Train your own image model in 5 minutes using your webcam. No code needed.
  • Ask Gemini: "Explain supervised learning with an example from a Vizag fish market."

+
  • Data — facts, numbers, text or images that a computer can store.
  • Model — the result of training; the "brain" that gives predictions.
  • Training — the process of learning from data.
  • Prediction — the answer a model gives for a new input.
  • Label — the correct answer attached to a piece of data.
  • Pattern — something that repeats in data.
  • Neural network — a model made of many small connected units (neurons).
  • Layer — a group of neurons in a network.
  • GPU — Graphics Processing Unit; a chip that is very fast at the maths AI needs.

+

Unit I · Introduction to AI Tools

+

Old AI mainly classified things. Is this a cat or a dog? Is this email spam or not?

+

Generative AI is different. It creates new things. It can write a poem, draw a picture, compose music, make a video or write a program. The word generate means to make.
+"Write a poem about Rushikonda beach"A new poem
+"A fishing boat at sunrise, oil painting"A new image
+"Write a C program to add two numbers"New code

+

An LLM is a Large Language Model. It is the engine inside ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude.

+
  • Large — it has billions of numbers (called parameters) inside it.
  • Language — it works with text: English, Telugu, Hindi, Python, C and more.
  • Model — it was trained on a huge amount of text from books and the internet.

+

An LLM does one thing. It guesses the next word.

+

Give it "Visakhapatnam is a city on the east". It guesses "coast". Add that and ask again. It guesses "of". Then "India". It keeps going, one word at a time, until the answer is complete.

+

That is all. But because it read so much text, its guesses are very good. It can answer questions, write essays and write code just by guessing the next word again and again.

+
Actually, the model works with tokens, not words. A token is a word or a part of a word. "Visakhapatnam" might be 4 tokens. You will see the word token in many AI tools.

+
  1. They can be wrong. An LLM does not "know" facts. It guesses what sounds right. Sometimes it makes up things that are false. This is called a hallucination. Always check important facts.
  2. They have a cut-off date. The model learned from text up to some date. It may not know last month's news. Some tools fix this by searching the web.
  3. They have a context window. This is how much text the model can read at one time. If you paste a very long document, the model may forget the start.
  4. They are not alive. An LLM has no feelings, no opinions and no memory of you (unless the app saves your chat).
  5. Same question, different answers. LLMs use a little randomness. Ask twice and you may get two different answers.

+
  • Image models make pictures from text. Examples: Imagen (Google), DALL·E and GPT Image (OpenAI), Midjourney, Stable Diffusion.
  • Audio models make speech or music. Examples: ElevenLabs, Suno.
  • Video models make short videos. Examples: Veo (Google), Sora (OpenAI).
  • Multimodal models can handle text, images, audio and video together. Gemini and GPT are multimodal. You can show them a photo and ask a question about it.

+
  • In Gemini or ChatGPT, type only: "Visakhapatnam is a city on the" and see how it continues the sentence.
  • Upload a photo of your handwritten notes to Gemini and ask it to type them out.
  • See how text becomes tokens: OpenAI Tokenizer. Type your name and a Telugu word.
  • Short video: How LLMs work – 3Blue1Brown.

+
  • Generate — to make or create something new.
  • Classify — to put something into a group (cat or dog, spam or not spam).
  • LLM — Large Language Model; an AI trained on a huge amount of text.
  • Parameter — a number inside a model that was set during training.
  • Token — a word or part of a word; the unit an LLM reads and writes.
  • Hallucination — when an AI confidently gives a wrong or made-up answer.
  • Cut-off date — the last date of the data the model was trained on.
  • Context window — the amount of text a model can look at in one go.
  • Multimodal — can work with many types of input: text, image, audio, video.

+

  • Chatbots that answer customer questions 24 hours a day.

Unit I · Introduction to AI Tools

5. The tools: ChatGPT, Gemini, NotebookLM, AI Studio

+

This course uses four main tools. All of them are free to start. Make your accounts now.

+

Made by: OpenAI. Link: chatgpt.com

+

ChatGPT is the most famous AI chat tool. You type a question. It answers. You can continue the chat, and it remembers what you said earlier in the same chat.

+

Good for: writing, explaining, coding, brainstorming, images.

+

How to start: Go to the link. Sign up with your Gmail. Type in the box at the bottom. Press Enter.

+
  • Click the + button to upload a file or image.
  • Use the microphone icon to speak instead of typing.
  • Start a new chat for a new topic. Old chats are saved on the left side.

+

Made by: Google. Link: gemini.google.com

+

Gemini is Google's AI chat tool. It works like ChatGPT. It is built into many Google products: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides and Android phones.

+

Good for: everything ChatGPT does, plus working with Google Docs, Drive and YouTube. It is strong in Indian languages, including Telugu.

+
  • Gems — you can make your own custom helper with a fixed set of instructions. For example, a "C Lab Helper" Gem.
  • Deep Research — Gemini reads many web pages and writes a long report.
  • Can look at YouTube videos and summarise them.
  • Can make images and short videos.

+

Made by: Google. Link: notebooklm.google.com

+

NotebookLM is different. It does not answer from the internet. It answers only from the documents you upload. These are called sources. You can upload PDFs, Google Docs, websites, YouTube links and audio.

+

Good for: studying your textbooks and notes. It does not hallucinate much, because every answer points back to your source.

+
  • Ask questions about your uploaded PDF. Every answer shows which page it came from.
  • Audio Overview — makes a podcast where two voices discuss your document. Great for revising on the bus.
  • Makes a study guide, FAQ, timeline or mind map in one click.

+

Made by: Google. Link: aistudio.google.com

+

Google AI Studio is for people who want to see how the model works under the hood. It is the developer's view of Gemini. Gemini the app is like a car. AI Studio is like the engine with the bonnet open.

+

Good for: experimenting, building a small AI app, getting an API key.

+
  • Choose different Gemini models and compare them.
  • Set a system instruction. This is a rule the model always follows, like "Always answer in Telugu".
  • Change the temperature. Low = more exact. High = more creative.
  • The Build section can create a small web app from your description.
  • Get a free API key to use Gemini from your own Python program.
+ChatGPTIts training + web searchGeneral chat, writing, code
+GeminiIts training + Google search + your Google appsGeneral chat, Google Docs, Indian languages
+NotebookLMOnly your uploaded filesStudy, summaries, questions about your notes
+AI StudioGemini models, with your settingsExperiments, building apps, API keys

+
  • Claude by Anthropic — very good for writing and coding.
  • Microsoft Copilot — built into Windows, Edge and Office.
  • Perplexity — an AI search engine with sources.
  • Meta AI — inside WhatsApp and Instagram.

+

This is Lab experiment 1. Ask the same question in all four tools and compare.

+
prompt
Explain how a lithium-ion battery works, for a first year engineering student. Use simple English. Give 5 bullet points.

+
  • Open ChatGPT, Gemini and AI Studio. Paste the prompt. Save all three answers in a document.
  • Open NotebookLM. Add a Wikipedia page about lithium-ion batteries as a source. Ask the same question.
  • Which answer was the simplest? Which was the most correct? Which one showed sources?

+
  • Account — your personal login for a website.
  • Chat — a conversation; in AI tools, one conversation is saved as one chat.
  • Upload — to send a file from your computer to a website.
  • Source — a document that an answer comes from.
  • Custom — made for one specific purpose.
  • System instruction — a rule given to the AI before the chat starts.
  • Temperature — a setting that controls how random or creative the AI answers are.
  • API key — a secret code that lets your own program use an AI service.
  • Under the hood — the inside workings of something (like under the bonnet of a car).

+

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
entries.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
entries.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. Inside browser_batch, navigate (and other tools that act on a page) requires an explicit tabId. Pass an explicit tabId when you need a specific tab or when the session's group has multiple tabs whose state you must preserve. tabId is required for url:"back"/"forward". A tab opened for you this way is yours to clean up, the same as one from tabs_create_mcp: close it with tabs_close_mcp once you no longer need it and before finishing your task, unless the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

tabId.description: Tab ID to navigate. Must be a tab in the current group. If omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate standalone, tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you. Required for url:"back"/"forward" and for navigate (and other tools that act on a page) inside browser_batch.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__resize_window
entries.description: Resize the current browser window to specified dimensions. Useful for testing responsive designs or setting up specific screen sizes. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.

tabId.description: Tab ID to get the window for. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
entries.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
entries.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
entries.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

entries.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__browser_batch
entries.description: Execute a sequence of browser tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — if an action navigates to a domain without permission, the next item's check fails and the batch stops. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested.

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, tabs_create_mcp). browser_batch cannot be nested.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","coordinate":[100,200],"tabId":123}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello","tabId":123}},{"name":"navigate","input":{"url":"https://example.com","tabId":123}}]

content.text:
The book is written, built, checked in the browser, and pushed to `main` (commit `088c2c2`). Since `docs/` is the GitHub Pages root, it should be live in a minute or two at **https://aikaryashala.github.io/gvpihlr/ai-tools/** (or `/ai-tools/` under your custom domain, if you have one set).

## What's there

**21 chapters + a lab guide**, in simple English with short sentences, each ending with a **Try it** box (links to experiment) and a **New words** box:

| Unit | Chapters |
|---|---|
| I · Introduction | What is AI · How AI learns · Generative AI and LLMs · Where it's used · The four tools · Responsible AI |
| II · Prompt engineering | Writing good prompts · Types of prompts · Writing & summarizing · Documents for a context · Greeting cards (Canva) |
| III · Coding | Generating code · Debugging with a second tool · Converting languages · Test cases |
| IV · Presentations | Gamma · Gemini + Google Slides · Audio, video, animation, music |
| V · Applications | AI-enabled apps · Workflow automation · Future trends |
| Appendix | Lab guide: all 20 experiments → chapter, tools, what to put in the record, plus every link in one place |

Examples use Vizag context throughout (RK Beach, Araku bus, Simhachalam steps, steel plant, port, KGH, Anakapalle farmers, GVPIHLR notices).

## How it's built

- `book/*.md` — the source. Edit these.
- `python3 tools/build_book.py` — rebuilds `docs/ai-tools/` (no dependencies; it has its own tiny Markdown converter).
- `tools/book_template.html` + `docs/ai-tools/book.css` — layout: sticky chapter sidebar on desktop, collapsible "Chapters" box on phones, prev/next at the bottom.

## Home page changes

The last commit deleted `docs/c-lab/`, but the home page still linked to it. I replaced the C Lab nav link and card with the book, and the "Material: Coming soon" box now links to the book.

One leftover you may want to fix separately: `docs/codexray/index.html` (generated from `tools/codexray_template.html`) still links to `../c-lab/c-lab.css` and has a "C Lab" nav link.
